title: What OSINT is, and where the legal line sits
objective: Explain OSINT, passive collection and the legal limits of an investigator.

questions.q: What does OSINT stand for?
options: Open-Source Intelligence — intelligence built from publicly available information
questions.explain: "Open source" here means open to the public (websites, social media, public records), not open-source software.

questions.q: Which of these is PASSIVE collection?
options: Reading a public social-media profile without logging in to anyone's account
Guessing the password of the subject's email
Sending the subject a fake friend request to see private posts
questions.explain: Passive means you only look at what is already public and never touch or trick the target.

questions.q: You find the login page of a suspect's private account. What may an OSINT investigator do?
options: Record that the account exists and stop there
Use a leaked password found in a breach dump
Reset the password using the "forgot password" link
questions.explain: Entering an account without permission is unauthorised access, a crime, even if your intention is good.

questions.q: In India, accessing a computer, account or camera without permission is an offence under:
options: No law, if the intention is good
questions.explain: Section 43 covers unauthorised access and Section 66 makes it a punishable offence when done dishonestly; good intent is not a defence.

questions.q: A crime-branch officer needs CCTV footage from a shop near where a girl was last seen. The correct way is:
options: Request it from the owner, backed by a legal notice if needed
Hack the shop's DVR over the internet
questions.explain: Police obtain footage through consent or legal notice so that it is lawful and usable in court.

questions.q: What is the difference between information and intelligence?
options: Intelligence is information that has been verified and analysed to answer a specific question
questions.explain: A pile of screenshots is information; "she was last seen at this bus stand at 6 pm, confirmed by two sources" is intelligence.

questions.q: The intelligence cycle runs in which order?
questions.explain: You decide the question first, then collect, clean up, analyse and finally report.

questions.q: Why do investigators use a separate research browser profile and account instead of their personal one?
options: So their identity is not exposed and they do not tip off the subject by an accidental like or view
To hide from their own employer
questions.explain: This is operational security (OPSEC); one accidental "like" from your real account can alert the subject.

questions.q: In a red-team engagement, OSINT belongs to which phase?
questions.explain: Red teams use the same OSINT skills to map a client's people and systems before any attack, always inside an agreed scope.

questions.q: Print the current date and time in UTC, to timestamp a line in your case notes.
questions.explain: Investigators log in UTC so that times from different sources and time zones can be compared.

questions.q: Save the page https://example.com to a file named page.html for your evidence folder.
questions.explain: Pages change or get deleted, so you save a copy at the moment you see it.

labs.title: Write your own ground rules
labs.scenario: Before any practice, write a short rules page for yourself: what you will do, what you will never do, and who gets your findings in a real case.
steps: # I only use information that is public
# I never log in to, guess or reset another person's account
# I never contact the subject, their family or friends
# I never publish what I find; findings in a real case go to the police
# I practise on myself, on consenting friends, or in organised events
verify: every rule keeps you passive and inside the law

labs.title: Set up a case folder and log
labs.scenario: Create a tidy workspace for a practice case, with an evidence folder, a notes folder and a log that records the UTC time of everything you do.
hints: Brace expansion makes both folders in one command.
verify: the log shows a UTC timestamp and both folders exist

labs.title: OSINT yourself
labs.scenario: You are the safest legal target. Search your own full name, usernames, phone number and email, and list everything a stranger could learn about you.
hints: Use a private window so results are not personalised.
steps: # search "your full name" in quotes, then with your city and college
# search each username you have ever used
# note every result: photo, address, phone, school, relatives
# tighten privacy settings or delete what you do not want public
verify: you have a written list of what is exposed and what you fixed

title: Search operators, archives and checking viral claims
objective: Use advanced search operators and verify a claim before trusting it.

questions.q: What does the operator site:example.com do?
options: Limits results to pages on example.com
questions.explain: site: narrows a search to one website or domain, which removes most of the noise.

questions.q: Putting a phrase in "double quotes" makes the search engine:
options: Match that exact phrase in that exact order
questions.explain: Exact-phrase search is the quickest way to find a specific name or sentence.

questions.q: A minus sign before a word, as in jaguar -car, does what?
questions.explain: Excluding words removes a whole unwanted meaning from the results.

questions.q: What does filetype:pdf (or ext:pdf) do?
options: Finds pages that mention the word pdf
questions.explain: Documents often carry more detail than web pages, including author names and dates.

questions.q: A post you need was deleted yesterday. Where do you look first?
options: The Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) and other web archives
questions.explain: Archives store old snapshots of pages, so deleted or edited content can often still be seen.

questions.q: A reel claims "123 girls were kidnapped in this city in 22 hours". What is the correct first step?
options: Look for the original source and an official statement before believing or forwarding it
Forward it to every group to warn people
Assume it is true because it has many views
Add a bigger number and repost
questions.explain: Verification means finding who first said it and whether official records support it; view counts prove nothing.

questions.q: A photo is shared as "taken today at the incident". The fastest way to test that is:
options: Reverse image search to see whether the photo appeared online earlier
Ask the person who forwarded it
Zoom in until it looks real
questions.explain: Old photos are constantly reused for new events; an earlier copy online disproves "taken today".

questions.q: Two news sites report the same claim, but both quote the same single viral audio clip. How many independent sources do you have?
options: None, news is never a source
questions.explain: Sources are independent only if they got the information separately; copies of one clip count once.

questions.q: Write a search that returns only PDF files from the site example.com.
questions.explain: Combining operators narrows results sharply; each one removes more noise.

questions.q: Write a search for the exact phrase missing person, only on the site example.com.
questions.explain: Quotes fix the phrase and site: fixes the place.

questions.q: Write a search for pages on example.com that have the word login in their URL.
questions.explain: inurl: matches text in the address itself; red teams use it in recon to find login portals of an authorised target.

labs.title: Find public documents with operators
labs.scenario: Using only search operators, list the public PDF notices on your own college's website and note what each reveals (names, dates, phone numbers).
hints: Public documents only; do not try to open anything that asks for a login.
steps: # for each result, note what personal details are visible
verify: you found documents without touching any login page

labs.title: Fact-check a viral claim
labs.scenario: Pick one alarming forward you received recently. Trace it back and decide whether it is true, false or unproven. Write your reasoning in five lines.
steps: # 1 write the claim as one exact sentence
# 2 search the sentence in quotes to find the earliest post
# 3 reverse-search any photo or video frame
# 4 look for an official statement or a named, accountable source
# 5 count independent sources and state your confidence
verify: your conclusion names the earliest source and the evidence for it

labs.title: See an older version of a page
labs.scenario: Open the Wayback Machine, look up a site you know well, and compare a snapshot from a few years ago with today's page.
steps: # open web.archive.org and enter the address
# pick a year, then a highlighted date on the calendar
# copy the archive link: it is a stable reference for a report
verify: you have an archive link showing the older content

title: Finding people and the missing-person workflow
objective: Pivot between identifiers and follow the rules for missing-person OSINT.

questions.q: What is "pivoting" in OSINT?
options: Using one found identifier, such as a username, to discover the next one
questions.explain: A username leads to a profile, the profile to a photo, the photo to a location; each find is a step to the next.

questions.q: Why is username reuse so useful to an investigator?
options: People often use the same handle on many sites, linking their accounts together
Sites share usernames with police automatically
questions.explain: One distinctive handle can connect accounts the person never meant to link.

questions.q: You search a common name and get 40 profiles. How do you decide which is your subject?
options: Confirm with at least two independent identifiers, such as city, college, photo or friends
Pick the one with most followers
questions.explain: Common names cause false matches, and a false match can harm an innocent person.

questions.q: A breach-check site such as Have I Been Pwned tells you:
options: Whether an email address appears in known data breaches
The current password of the account
questions.explain: It shows exposure, not passwords; and logging in with any leaked password would be a crime.

questions.q: In a Trace Labs missing-person event, contacting the missing person's family or friends is:
options: Forbidden; collection must be passive with zero contact
questions.explain: Contact can frighten the family, alert a kidnapper or damage the police investigation.

questions.q: Who should receive what you find about a real missing person?
options: The police or the organisers who pass it to police
questions.explain: Posting findings publicly can endanger the person and spread mistakes; police can verify and act.

questions.q: Which finding helps a missing-person case most?
options: Recent activity that shows where the person was after they were reported missing
Their school marks from five years ago
The number of followers they have
questions.explain: Fresh, location-related information is what moves a search forward.

questions.q: Someone close to you has actually gone missing. What should happen first?
options: Report to the police immediately (dial 112; 1098 for a child)
Start your own online investigation first
Post their photo in every group and wait
questions.explain: There is no 24-hour waiting rule; the first hours matter most, and OSINT only supports the police.

questions.q: Publishing a private person's address and phone number online is called:
options: Doxxing, and it is harmful and can be illegal
questions.explain: OSINT findings go to those with authority to act, never to the public.

questions.q: Check which websites have an account named demo_user123, using Sherlock.
questions.explain: Sherlock only checks whether a public profile page exists for that name on each site; it does not log in.

questions.q: Compute the SHA-256 hash of screenshot.png so you can later prove it was not altered.
questions.explain: The hash is a fingerprint of the file; if even one pixel changes later, the hash will be different.

labs.title: Pivot from your own username
labs.scenario: Start from one username you use. Without logging in anywhere, see how many of your own accounts a stranger could link together.
hints: Practise only on your own handle or a friend who agreed.
steps: # open each hit and confirm it is really you (photo, bio, city)
# note every new identifier it exposes: email, other handles, links
# repeat once from one newly found identifier
verify: you drew a small map: username -> accounts -> new identifiers

labs.title: Fill a subject profile sheet
labs.scenario: Make a one-page template for a missing-person case and fill it for a fictional person: basic details, online accounts, friends, last-seen day, and the source of every line.
steps: # Subject: name, age, city, physical description
# Accounts: platform, handle, link, last activity date
# Last seen: date, time, place, who reported it
# Every line: source link + UTC time you captured it
# Confidence for each line: confirmed / probable / unverified
verify: no line in the sheet is missing a source

labs.title: Read the rules of a real event
labs.scenario: Open the Trace Labs website and read the rules and scoring categories for their Search Party events. Summarise in your notes what is allowed and what is not.
steps: # note the "no contact" rule in your own words
# list the categories of information that earn points
# note which categories score highest and why
# write down who receives the findings afterwards
verify: you can explain why contact with the subject is banned

title: Photos, metadata and working out a location
objective: Extract image metadata and geolocate a photo from visual clues.

questions.q: What is EXIF data?
options: Hidden details stored inside a photo file, such as camera model, date, time and sometimes GPS position
The caption written under a post
questions.explain: The camera writes this metadata automatically; most people never know it is there.

questions.q: You download a photo from Instagram or WhatsApp and it has no GPS data. The most likely reason is:
options: Most social platforms remove metadata when a photo is uploaded
The phone has no GPS chip
GPS data expires after a week
questions.explain: Platforms strip EXIF on upload, so original files (email, cloud, a seized phone) are far richer than reposts.

questions.q: What is reverse image search used for?
options: Finding where else, and how early, the same image appears online
Flipping an image left to right
questions.explain: It finds the original source and earlier copies, which exposes reused or stolen photos.

questions.q: A photo has no metadata. Which clue helps most to work out where it was taken?
options: Text on signs and shopfronts, such as language, phone codes and shop names
The colour of the person's shirt
questions.explain: Readable text narrows a location quickly: script gives the region, a phone code gives the city.

questions.q: What can shadows in an outdoor photo tell you?
options: The rough direction of the sun, and so the approximate time of day
questions.explain: Working out time from shadows is called chronolocation; a photo with long shadows was not taken at noon.

questions.q: You think a photo was taken at a certain junction. How do you confirm it?
options: Match fixed features such as buildings, poles and signboards against satellite or street-level imagery
Check if the weather looks similar
questions.explain: Confirmation needs several fixed features lining up, not one similar-looking object.

questions.q: Why should you strip metadata from your own photos before posting them publicly?
options: It can reveal your home location and device to strangers
questions.explain: What helps an investigator also helps a stalker; this is the defensive side of the same skill.

questions.q: GPS coordinates inside a photo's EXIF data should be treated as:
options: A strong lead that still needs confirming, because metadata can be edited
questions.explain: Metadata is easy to change, so it is corroborated with visual clues or other evidence.

questions.q: Show all metadata stored in the file photo.jpg.
questions.explain: With no options, exiftool prints every tag it can read from the file.

questions.q: Show only the GPS tags of photo.jpg.
questions.explain: Asking for one tag group saves reading through a hundred lines of camera settings.

questions.q: Remove all metadata from photo.jpg before you share it.
questions.explain: Setting every tag to "nothing" clears them; exiftool keeps the original as photo.jpg_original.

labs.title: Read your own photo's metadata
labs.scenario: Copy a photo straight from your phone (by cable or email, not WhatsApp) and find out what it reveals about you.
hints: Send the same photo to yourself on WhatsApp and compare.
verify: you can state the device, the time and whether location was stored

labs.title: Strip and compare
labs.scenario: Remove the metadata from a copy of your photo and prove that it is gone.
verify: the GPS and camera tags are gone and the two hashes differ

labs.title: Geolocate one of your old photos
labs.scenario: Pick an old outdoor photo of your own with the location turned off. Using only what is visible, find the exact spot on a map and write down each clue you used.
hints: Start wide (country, city) and narrow down.
steps: # list readable text: signs, shop names, number plates, phone codes
# list fixed features: buildings, towers, hills, road layout
# search the text, then open the area in a map's satellite view
# match at least three fixed features before you call it confirmed
verify: you can point to the spot and name three matching features

title: Domains, IP addresses and email headers
objective: Map an organisation's public internet footprint using passive lookups.

questions.q: What does a WHOIS lookup show?
options: Registration details of a domain: registrar, dates and sometimes the owner
questions.explain: WHOIS is the public registration record; privacy services often hide the owner's name.

questions.q: Which DNS record type lists the mail servers of a domain?
questions.explain: MX means mail exchanger; A maps a name to an IP, NS lists name servers, PTR maps an IP back to a name.

questions.q: Certificate transparency logs (searched through crt.sh) are useful in recon because they:
options: Reveal subdomains that have been issued TLS certificates
Let you issue certificates for the target
questions.explain: Every public certificate is logged, so names like vpn.example.com appear without touching the target at all.

questions.q: An IP address geolocates to "Pune". What does that actually tell you?
options: Roughly where the internet provider's equipment is, not a house address
The exact flat of the user
questions.explain: Only the internet provider can link an IP and time to a subscriber, and it does so on a legal request from police.

questions.q: In an email's full headers, the "Received:" lines are read:
options: From the bottom upward, because each server adds its line on top
questions.explain: The lowest Received line is closest to the sender, so the trail starts at the bottom.

questions.q: SPF, DKIM and DMARC results in an email header tell you:
options: Whether the message really came from a server allowed to send for that domain
Whether the email has been read
questions.explain: A "fail" here is a strong sign that the sender address was forged.

questions.q: Shodan shows an internet-exposed camera at an address. Which action is legal for you?
options: Noting that it is exposed and reporting it
Logging in with the default password to "check"
Changing its settings to secure it
questions.explain: Seeing that a device is listed is passive; logging in to it is unauthorised access under the IT Act.

questions.q: Which of these is ACTIVE and therefore needs written authorisation?
options: Running an nmap scan against the organisation's servers
Reading the company's public job adverts
questions.explain: Active recon sends traffic to the target; red teams do it only inside an agreed scope.

questions.q: Look up the registration record of example.com.
questions.explain: WHOIS queries a public registry database, not the target's own servers.

questions.q: List the mail servers of example.com.
questions.explain: DNS is a public directory; mail servers hint at which email provider the organisation uses.

questions.q: Find the hostname that the IP address 8.8.8.8 points back to (a reverse lookup).
questions.explain: A reverse lookup asks for the PTR record, which often names the owner or provider.

labs.title: Passive footprint of a domain
labs.scenario: Using passive lookups only, build a one-page footprint of example.com (or a domain you own): registration, name servers, mail servers and IP address.
hints: Nothing here sends traffic to the target's own servers except normal DNS.
verify: you can say who registered it, where it is hosted and who handles its mail

labs.title: Subdomains from certificate logs
labs.scenario: List subdomains of example.com from public certificate transparency logs, without sending anything to the target.
hints: jq pulls one field out of JSON; sort -u removes duplicates.
verify: you have a de-duplicated list of names from the logs

labs.title: Trace an email you received
labs.scenario: Open the full headers ("Show original") of an email in your own inbox, ideally a spam message, and work out where it really came from.
steps: # read the Received lines bottom to top; note the first outside IP
verify: you can state the sending network and whether SPF and DKIM passed

title: Evidence, hashing and chain of custody
objective: Explain how digital evidence is kept trustworthy from seizure to court.

questions.q: What is the main goal of digital forensics?
options: To recover and present digital evidence in a way a court can trust
To speed up a slow computer
questions.explain: Finding the data is half the job; proving that nobody changed it is the other half.

questions.q: Locard's exchange principle says:
questions.explain: A person who uses a device leaves logs, timestamps and files behind, and that is what you look for.

questions.q: What is a chain of custody?
options: A written record of who held the evidence, when, and what they did with it
questions.explain: If there is a gap in the record, the defence can argue that the evidence was tampered with.

questions.q: Why is a hash taken as soon as evidence is collected?
options: To prove later that the evidence has not changed since then
questions.explain: The same data always gives the same hash, so a matching hash later proves the data is unchanged.

questions.q: One bit of a 500 GB disk image is changed. Its SHA-256 hash will:
options: Change in its last digit only
questions.explain: A tiny change in the input changes the whole hash, which is why any tampering shows.

questions.q: Why do examiners work on a copy and never on the original device?
options: Any use of the original can change it and damage its value as evidence
questions.explain: Even opening a file updates timestamps; the original is sealed and analysis happens on verified copies.

questions.q: What does a write blocker do?
options: Lets the examiner read a disk while preventing any change to it
questions.explain: Simply connecting a disk to a normal computer can alter it; the write blocker makes that impossible.

questions.q: "Order of volatility" means you collect which evidence first?
options: The data that disappears soonest, such as memory, before disk
questions.explain: RAM is lost at power-off while a disk keeps its data, so memory is captured first on a running machine.

questions.q: In Indian courts, an electronic record is admitted with a certificate under:
options: Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (earlier Section 65B of the Evidence Act)
questions.explain: The certificate states how the record was produced and that the device was working properly.

questions.q: Compute the SHA-256 hash of evidence.img.
questions.explain: This is the fingerprint you write on the custody form.

questions.q: Save the SHA-256 hash of evidence.img into a file named evidence.img.sha256.
questions.explain: Storing the hash beside the image lets anyone re-check it later.

questions.q: Check evidence.img against the hash saved in evidence.img.sha256.
questions.explain: The -c option recomputes the hash and prints OK or FAILED.

labs.title: Prove tampering with a hash
labs.scenario: Create a small "evidence" file, hash it, change a single character, and show that the hash exposes the change.
steps: echo "Meeting at 6 pm near the bus stand" > note.txt
verify: the first check prints OK and the second prints FAILED

labs.title: Fill a chain-of-custody form
labs.scenario: Design a simple custody form and fill it in for a pen drive that you "seize" from your own desk.
steps: # item: description, make, serial number, capacity
# collected: date, UTC time, place, by whom
# hash: algorithm and value of the image
# transfers: from, to, date, time, purpose, signature
# storage: where it is kept and who has access
verify: every moment of the item's life is covered by one line

labs.title: Plan for a running laptop
labs.scenario: You arrive and find a suspect's laptop switched on and unlocked. Write the order in which you would collect evidence and why.
hints: Think about what vanishes at power-off.
steps: # 1 photograph the screen and note the time
# 2 capture memory (RAM) to an external drive
# 3 record running processes and network connections
# 4 only then power down and image the disk through a write blocker
# 5 hash everything and start the custody form
verify: memory is collected before the disk, and every step is documented

title: Disk imaging and recovering deleted files
objective: Create a forensic image and recover deleted files from it.

questions.q: How is a forensic image different from copying files with a file manager?
options: It copies every bit of the disk, including deleted and unused areas
questions.explain: Deleted files live in space that a normal copy ignores, so only a bit-for-bit image preserves them.

questions.q: When a file is deleted normally, what usually happens?
options: Its entry is marked free but the content stays on disk until overwritten
Its content is wiped at once
questions.explain: Deleting removes the pointer, not the data, which is why recovery is often possible.

questions.q: Why is an evidence image mounted read-only?
options: So that looking at it cannot change it
To hide it from other users
questions.explain: A normal mount can update timestamps and journals, which would change the hash.

questions.q: A file named holiday.txt begins with the bytes FF D8 FF. What is it really?
options: A JPEG image with a changed extension
questions.explain: The first bytes (the signature or "magic number") identify the real type; the extension is only a label.

questions.q: What is file carving?
options: Recovering files from raw data by searching for their signatures, without using the file system
Splitting a large file into parts
questions.explain: Carving works even when the file system is damaged or the file's entry is gone.

questions.q: In the dd option conv=noerror,sync, the purpose is to:
options: Keep going past unreadable sectors and pad them, so the image keeps its correct layout
questions.explain: A failing disk should not stop the whole acquisition, and padding keeps every later byte in the right place.

questions.q: In Sleuth Kit, the command fls is used to:
options: List file and directory names in an image, including deleted ones
questions.explain: Deleted entries are marked with an asterisk, and each has a number you pass to icat to extract it.

questions.q: After imaging, the hash of the image is compared with the hash of the source disk in order to:
options: Prove that the image is an exact copy
questions.explain: Matching hashes are what let a court accept the copy in place of the original.

questions.q: Make a bit-for-bit image of the disk /dev/sdb in a file named evidence.img.
accept: dd if=/dev/sdb of=evidence.img bs=4M conv=noerror,sync status=progress
sudo dd if=/dev/sdb of=evidence.img bs=4M conv=noerror,sync status=progress
sudo dd if=/dev/sdb of=evidence.img bs=4M status=progress
questions.explain: if= is the input (source) and of= is the output; swapping them would overwrite the evidence.

questions.q: Mount evidence.img read-only on the directory /mnt/evidence.
questions.explain: loop treats the file as a disk and ro makes it read-only.

questions.q: Identify the real type of mystery.dat from its content, not its name.
questions.explain: The file command reads the signature at the start of the file.

questions.q: List only the deleted entries in disk.img, going through all folders, with Sleuth Kit.
questions.explain: -r recurses into folders and -d shows deleted entries only.

labs.title: Delete a file and recover it
labs.scenario: Build a small practice disk image, put a picture on it, delete the picture, then recover it from the image. Kali has these tools preinstalled.
hints: FAT is used because deleted files are easy to recover from it.
steps: sudo mkdir -p /mnt/practice && sudo mount -o loop practice.img /mnt/practice
sudo cp test.jpg /mnt/practice/ && sudo rm /mnt/practice/test.jpg && sudo umount /mnt/practice
verify: the two hashes match, proving the deleted file was fully recovered

labs.title: Unmask a disguised file
labs.scenario: Rename a JPEG to notes.txt, then prove what it really is in two different ways.
steps: # the first bytes ff d8 ff are the JPEG signature
verify: both file and the hex dump show it is a JPEG

labs.title: Carve files from an image
labs.scenario: Use a carving tool to pull pictures out of practice.img without relying on the file system.
hints: Carving finds files by signature, so the names will be lost.
verify: at least one JPEG is recovered in the carved folder

title: Timestamps, timelines and Linux logs
objective: Reconstruct what happened on a Linux system from timestamps and logs.

questions.q: In file timestamps, what does "mtime" record?
options: When the file's content was last modified
When the file was last read
questions.explain: mtime follows the content; atime is the last read and ctime is the last change to the file's metadata.

questions.q: On Linux, "ctime" means:
options: The last change to the file's metadata, such as permissions, owner or name
The time in the C locale
The time the file was copied
questions.explain: ctime is often mistaken for creation time; the birth time is a separate field.

questions.q: Why are investigation timelines written in UTC?
options: Evidence from different devices and time zones can then be compared directly
UTC is the Indian time zone
questions.explain: A phone, a server and a CCTV recorder may each use a different clock setting; UTC is the common reference.

questions.q: On a RHEL system, where are SSH login successes and failures logged?
questions.explain: RHEL uses /var/log/secure; Debian and Ubuntu use /var/log/auth.log; journalctl shows the same events.

questions.q: Which command shows FAILED login attempts?
questions.explain: lastb reads /var/log/btmp (failed logins); last reads /var/log/wtmp (successful ones).

questions.q: A log shows 400 "Failed password" lines from one IP and then one "Accepted password". What happened?
options: A brute-force attack that finally succeeded
A normal user who forgot the password once
questions.explain: Many failures followed by a success from the same source is the typical pattern of password guessing.

questions.q: Why is ~/.bash_history weak evidence on its own?
options: The user can edit or clear it, and it normally has no timestamps
It is deleted at every boot
questions.explain: It is a useful lead, but it must be supported by logs that the user cannot easily change.

questions.q: Someone used touch to backdate a file's mtime to last year. What often gives it away?
options: The ctime, which shows the moment the metadata was actually changed
questions.explain: An ordinary user cannot set ctime, so an old mtime with a very recent ctime is suspicious.

questions.q: After a break-in, which place should be checked for a hidden way back in?
options: Cron jobs, new user accounts and ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
questions.explain: Attackers leave persistence; red teams plant the same things, so knowing where defenders look helps both sides.

questions.q: Show all timestamps of the file report.pdf.
questions.explain: stat prints the access, modify, change and birth times together.

questions.q: Show the history of successful logins on this system.
questions.explain: last reads /var/log/wtmp, newest first.

questions.q: Print every failed SSH password attempt recorded in /var/log/secure.
questions.explain: Each matching line contains the user name tried and the source IP.

questions.q: Show today's log entries for the sshd service using journalctl.
questions.explain: -u selects one service and --since limits the time window.

questions.q: Find files under /home that were modified in the last 24 hours.
questions.explain: -mtime -1 means "less than one day ago"; recently changed files show what the intruder touched.

labs.title: Audit logins on your own VM
labs.scenario: Treat your own RHEL VM as the scene. List who logged in, who failed, and from where.
hints: Generate some data first: type a wrong password once over SSH.
verify: you can say when the failed attempt happened and from which address

labs.title: Rank attackers by failed logins
labs.scenario: Build a one-line pipeline that counts failed SSH logins per source IP, highest first.
hints: In a "Failed password" line the IP is the fourth field from the end.
steps: sudo grep "Failed password" /var/log/secure | awk '{print $(NF-3)}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head
# read it as: count, then IP address
verify: the output is a ranked list of IPs with counts

labs.title: Catch a backdated file
labs.scenario: Backdate a file with touch and show that one timestamp still tells the truth.
verify: Modify shows the fake date while Change shows the real moment of tampering

title: Memory and network forensics
objective: Triage a memory image and a packet capture for evidence of activity.

questions.q: Why is RAM captured before a running computer is shut down?
options: It holds running processes, network connections and keys that vanish at power-off
It is bigger than the disk
It is easier to read than a disk
questions.explain: Some evidence never touches the disk at all, such as unsaved chats and malware that runs only in memory.

questions.q: Which tool is used to analyse a memory image?
questions.explain: Volatility reads the operating system's own structures inside the dump to list processes, connections and more.

questions.q: In Volatility 3, windows.pslist shows:
options: The processes that were running when memory was captured
questions.explain: The process list is the usual first look: what was running, and when it started.

questions.q: A process called svchost.exe is running from a user's Downloads folder. This is suspicious because:
options: The real svchost.exe runs from the Windows system folder
questions.explain: Malware often borrows a trusted name; the wrong location or parent process gives it away.

questions.q: What is a PCAP file?
questions.explain: Tools such as tcpdump and Wireshark save captured traffic in this format for later analysis.

questions.q: The traffic in a capture is HTTPS. What can an analyst still see?
options: Who talked to whom, when, and how much, but not the content
questions.explain: Encryption hides content, but addresses, times, sizes and usually the site name remain visible.

questions.q: A CDR (call detail record) contains:
options: Numbers, times, durations and tower locations of calls, not the conversation
questions.explain: Police obtain CDRs from the telecom company by legal request; they show contacts and movement, not content.

questions.q: Which is a Wireshark display filter for traffic to or from the address 10.0.0.5?
questions.explain: Display filters use field names and ==; they hide packets on screen without deleting them from the capture.

questions.q: List the processes in the Windows memory image memory.raw with Volatility 3.
questions.explain: -f names the image and the plugin name says what to extract.

questions.q: Show the network connections recorded in memory.raw with Volatility 3.
questions.explain: netscan links each connection to the process that owned it.

questions.q: Capture traffic on the interface eth0 into the file capture.pcap.
questions.explain: -i picks the interface and -w writes raw packets to a file. Capture only on networks you own or are authorised to monitor.

questions.q: Read the packets stored in capture.pcap.
questions.explain: -r reads from a file instead of a live interface.

questions.q: Show only the DNS packets in capture.pcap using tshark.
questions.explain: -Y applies a display filter; DNS queries reveal which sites a machine tried to reach.

labs.title: Record and read your own traffic
labs.scenario: On your own VM, capture a minute of your own traffic while you open one website, then find the DNS lookup for it.
verify: you can point to the DNS query for example.com and the reply

labs.title: First look at a memory image
labs.scenario: Download a public practice memory image (for example from the MemLabs challenges) and answer: what system is it, what was running, and what was it talking to?
hints: Run the plugins in this order; each one narrows the next.
verify: you can name one process worth a closer look and say why

labs.title: Find a login sent in clear text
labs.scenario: In a practice capture that contains plain HTTP, find the request in which a form was submitted and see why HTTP is unsafe.
hints: Public practice captures are available on the Wireshark sample captures page.
steps: # in Wireshark: right-click the packet -> Follow -> TCP Stream
verify: you can show the submitted form fields in the stream

title: Windows, phones, CCTV and the final report
objective: Identify key artefacts on Windows and mobile devices and write up a case.

questions.q: Windows Security event ID 4625 means:
options: A new user account was created
questions.explain: 4625 is a failed logon and 4624 a successful one; many 4625s then a 4624 is the Windows brute-force pattern.

questions.q: Windows event ID 1102 in the Security log means:
questions.explain: Clearing the log is itself logged, so an attempt to hide tracks leaves its own trace.

questions.q: Which registry location records USB storage devices that were plugged in?
questions.explain: It stores the make, model and serial number of each device, which can tie a specific pen drive to a computer.

questions.q: Files in C:\Windows\Prefetch are evidence of:
options: Programs that were run, and when
questions.explain: Windows creates a prefetch file to speed up launches, so it also records that a program was executed.

questions.q: A phone is seized as evidence. Why is it put in airplane mode or a Faraday bag?
options: To stop a remote wipe and stop new data from changing it
To back it up to the cloud
questions.explain: A connected phone can be erased remotely and keeps changing as new messages arrive.

questions.q: A CCTV recorder's clock shows 10:42 when the real time is 10:30. The investigator must:
options: Record the 12-minute offset and correct every time taken from that footage
Change the recorder's clock and say nothing
questions.explain: Recorder clocks drift; an unrecorded offset can place a person at the wrong time.

questions.q: Police obtain CCTV footage from a private owner by:
options: Consent or a legal notice to produce it, then hashing and documenting the export
Taking a phone video of the screen only
questions.explain: A lawful request and a hashed, documented export make the footage usable in court.

questions.q: A good forensic report must be written so that:
options: Another examiner can repeat the steps and reach the same findings
Only the author can understand it
It contains opinions and no facts
questions.explain: Repeatability is what separates evidence from a personal claim.

questions.q: A red teamer benefits from knowing forensics because:
options: They learn what traces their actions leave and how defenders find them
It replaces the need for authorisation
It lets them skip the report
questions.explain: Knowing the defender's view makes you a better tester and gives clients better advice on detection.

questions.q: In PowerShell, compute the SHA-256 hash of evidence.img.
questions.explain: SHA256 is the default algorithm of Get-FileHash; certutil is the older built-in tool.

questions.q: List the Android devices connected to your computer over USB debugging.
questions.explain: adb is the Android Debug Bridge; examiners use it only on devices they have authority or consent to examine.

questions.q: List the tables inside the SQLite database file named History.
questions.explain: Browsers and chat apps store their data in SQLite files, so reading tables is a core skill.

labs.title: Audit logons on your own Windows PC
labs.scenario: On your own Windows machine, open PowerShell as administrator and list recent failed and successful logons.
hints: Lock the PC and type a wrong password once to create a 4625 event.
verify: you can find your own wrong-password attempt and its time

labs.title: Read your own browser history as a database
labs.scenario: Copy your own Chrome history file and read it with sqlite3, the way an examiner would on a seized image.
hints: Work on a copy; the live file is locked while the browser is open.
steps: sqlite3 History "SELECT url, title FROM urls ORDER BY last_visit_time DESC LIMIT 10;"
verify: the last ten sites you visited are listed from the copy

labs.title: Capstone: a missing-person case on paper
labs.scenario: A 16-year-old (fictional) is reported missing at 7 pm. Plan the digital side of the investigation from start to report, marking each step as OSINT, legal request or forensics.
hints: No step should involve breaking into anything.
steps: # OSINT: public profiles, last public activity, usernames, photos
# Legal request: phone location and CDR from the telecom company
# Legal request: CCTV from the bus stand and shops, hashed on export
# Forensics: her laptop imaged through a write blocker; chats and history read from the copy
# Timeline: all times in UTC, CCTV clock offsets corrected
# Report: facts, sources, hashes, confidence, and what is still unknown
verify: every step is lawful and every fact in the report has a source
